topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and states what students should learn.

topics.label: Genetic origins and cellular context of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations arise and enable cancer to evolve in a susceptible cell and a permissive microenvironment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risk and interpretation of causal evidence
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the contribution of environmental exposure to cancer risk and how evidence for that contribution should be interpreted.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infection can drive carcinogenesis, using Burkitt lymphoma as a detailed example.

topics.label: Mechanisms of DNA damage by environmental carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage capable of generating cancer-associated mutations.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish why mutational initiation may require a subsequent growth-promoting environment for tumours to develop.

topics.label: Developmental susceptibility and recap of carcinogenic mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: The discussion of developmental susceptibility completes the account of carcinogenic mechanisms, which the following subtopic recaps.

topics.label: Evidence linking carcinogen exposure to human cancers
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence collected from human populations and cancer genomes can link exposure to cancer development.

topics.label: Experimental carcinogenicity tests and their limitations
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics evaluate how experimental tests detect carcinogenic potential and why their results may not fully predict human cancer risk.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing recaps the lecture's conclusions and places them in the context of everyday risk–benefit decisions.
